_about: Facts for the results-first restructure (2026-10-05): new slides r-setup (what we reproduced, data, recipe), r-pretrain-claims (pre-training claims), r-finetune-claims (fine-tuning claims). Every number is verified against our BERT reproduction's results/runs.jsonl, results/summary.md, results/demo.json, results/viz_pretrain.json, ckpt/mini_*/log.json and the paper text (arXiv 1810.04805v2). Paper numbers: dev unless marked test. Our numbers: GLUE dev, mean +/- sample std over n seeds.

pretraining.data: BooksCorpus (800M words) + English Wikipedia (2,500M words) = 3.3 billion words
pretraining.steps: 1,000,000 steps of 256 sequences x 512 tokens, about 40 passes over the 3.3-billion-word corpus
pretraining.compute: BERT-base: 4 Cloud TPUs in Pod configuration (16 TPU chips total), 4 days
pretraining.what_we_did: NOT redone at full size: we use Google's released checkpoint google-bert/bert-base-uncased (110M parameters; 109,483,778 counted with an MRPC head). Its claims are tested at small scale (mini BERTs) and against GPT-1.

finetuning.paper_tasks: GLUE (8 tasks; WNLI excluded), SQuAD v1.1/v2.0, SWAG, CoNLL-2003 NER
finetuning.recipe: batch 32, 3 epochs, learning rate = best of {5e-5, 4e-5, 3e-5, 2e-5} on dev (Sec. 4.1); max length 128 in our runs
finetuning.what_we_did: Redone on 7 of the 8 GLUE tasks (no QQP; no SQuAD/SWAG/NER): batch 32 and 3 epochs as in the paper; learning rate fixed at 2e-5 (one of the paper's four candidates); the paper's full 4-rate search re-run only for MRPC and RTE

our_three_tracks.what: fine-tune the released BERT-base on 7 GLUE tasks with the paper's recipe, compare with the paper

pre-train 4-layer BERTs from scratch on WikiText-103 with different objectives (masked LM with/without NSP, left-to-right); fine-tune GPT-1 with the same loop; run the released model on the paper's own MLM/NSP examples
frozen features vs full fine-tuning; the 4-learning-rate search; BERT-Large stability on RTE

glue_data._source: Hugging Face nyu-mll/glue; sizes are n_train / n_eval from our runs. Test labels are hidden (GLUE evaluation server), so every score is on the dev set.

rows.asks: does the sentence answer the question?
how similar are A and B? (0-5)
do A and B mean the same?

glue_data.not_run: QQP (363k pairs; GLUE's 8th task in the paper)
glue_data.mnli_note: MNLI training data covers 5 genres; the matched dev set uses the same 5
glue_data.not_run_reason: QQP skipped by choice (not a technical limit): the paper reports QQP only as a test-server score (Table 1, F1 71.2; no dev number in Tables 5/6), so a dev run could not be compared; it is large (363k pairs, about one MNLI-sized run); and MRPC already covers paraphrase detection.

mini_pretraining.data: WikiText-103 (raw): 28,472 Wikipedia articles, 109,192,978 WordPiece tokens (bert-base-uncased vocabulary), 1,196,547 sentence pairs of up to 128 tokens
mini_pretraining.training: 20,000 steps x 256 pairs each; the same data, order and initial weights for every variant; only the objective differs
mini_pretraining.variants: mlm15_nsp (masked LM 15% + NSP), mlm15 (masked LM only), ltr (left-to-right LM, causal mask, no NSP), mlm40 (40% masking)

scale.fine_tuning_runs: 218 (222 rows in runs.jsonl minus 4 invalid frozen-head runs whose head never trained)
scale.gpu_hours: 8.9 in total: 6.85 h fine-tuning + 2.0 h mini pre-training, one RTX 5090 laptop GPU
scale.note: the summary slide said 209 runs / 8.7 h before the last 9 GPT-1 runs (CoLA x5, STS-B x3, one CoLA re-run); update it to 218 / 8.9

paper_examples._about: The paper's own MLM/NSP examples (Sec. 3.1 / Appendix A.1), run through the released pre-trained BERT-base heads (results/demo.json); GPT-1 contrast from results/viz_pretrain.json

mlm.input: the man went to the [MASK] to buy a gallon of milk.

nsp.a: the man went to the store.
nsp.b: he bought a gallon of milk.

nsp.a: the man went to the store.

paper_examples.verdict: the released model behaves as the paper describes

ablation_table5._about: Paper Table 5 (BERT-base, dev) vs our 4-layer BERTs (WikiText-103, dev; QNLI 2 seeds, SST-2 and MRPC 3 seeds). Compare DIRECTIONS, not sizes: our models are 10x smaller and trained on 30x less text.

rows.change: left-to-right instead of masked LM (both without NSP)

ablation_table5.verdict: Direction reproduced: dropping NSP hurts the pair tasks, and a left-to-right model loses a pair task (QNLI -11.2) but not the single-sentence task (SST-2). Not reproduced: the paper's big left-to-right drop is on MRPC (-9.0); ours is on QNLI, MRPC barely moves (small models, small data).

bert_vs_gpt1._about: Same fine-tuning loop, same dev sets. GPT-1 = openai-gpt with its paper's lr 6.25e-5. BERT = our BERT-base means. Paper Table 1 compares them on the TEST server.

rows.note: *4 of 5 seeds; seed 3 failed (MCC 0, all 'acceptable'; re-run failed again)
gap +4.0 (results/summary.md controls table); paper Table 1 test F1 88.9 vs 82.3 = +6.6

bert_vs_gpt1.verdict: Reproduced: BERT higher on all 6 tasks we ran both on. Caveat: GPT-1 was also pre-trained on less text (BooksCorpus only), so this compares the two released models, not attention direction alone.

features_vs_finetuning.paper: Sec. 5.3, Table 7, CoNLL-2003 NER dev F1: fine-tuning BERT-base 96.4; best feature-based (concat last four hidden layers, frozen) 96.1; gap 0.3. The paper's point: BERT is effective for BOTH approaches (features are almost as good).
features_vs_finetuning.ours: SST-2 dev accuracy: full fine-tuning 93.0 +/- 0.2 (3 seeds); best frozen features + logistic regression 86.8 (mean-pooled, last four layers concatenated); gap 6.2. MRPC: fine-tuning 84.1 vs best frozen-layer probe 76.0 (gap 8.1)
features_vs_finetuning.verdict: NOT reproduced for sentence classification: the paper finds frozen features almost as good as fine-tuning on NER (-0.3 F1); on SST-2 our best frozen features are 6.2 points behind fine-tuning (different task and a smaller probe training set, so this is a limit of the claim's scope, not a contradiction of the NER result).
features_vs_finetuning.caveats: our frozen-feature probe is logistic regression trained on a 20,000-sentence subsample of SST-2 train (fine-tuning used all 67,349), and 86.8 is the best of 27 layer/pooling combinations picked on dev; different task type (sentence classification vs NER tagging)

lr_search.paper: Sec. 4.1: for each task the best of {5e-5, 4e-5, 3e-5, 2e-5} on dev
lr_search.verdict: The search is worth +2.0 on MRPC and +1.8 on RTE, and it is chosen on the same dev set it is reported on, so the paper's small-task numbers are slightly optimistic.

bert_large_stability.paper: Sec. 4.1: 'for BERT-LARGE we found that fine-tuning was sometimes unstable on small datasets, so we ran several random restarts and selected the best model on the Dev set'
bert_large_stability.ours: BERT-Large on RTE, 6 seeds each, 3 epochs, lr 2e-5
bert_large_stability.collapse_meaning: predicts one class for every RTE pair, so accuracy = that class's share: 47.3 or 52.7
bert_large_stability.cause: Google's released BERT optimizer (AdamWeightDecayOptimizer) skips Adam's bias correction, so early updates are up to ~6x larger; Mosbach et al. (ICLR 2021) link the instability to this and to too few steps. The BERT paper itself does not mention bias correction.
bert_large_stability.verdict: Instability reproduced (4 of 6 runs collapse); adding bias correction removes it (0 of 6) and lifts the mean by 15.9.

summary_slide_fix: r-summary: '209' fine-tuning runs -> '218'; '8.7 GPU hours' -> '8.9 GPU hours'
notes_from_script_check: GPT-1 ran through the same fine-tuning LOOP but with its own lr 6.25e-5 and 0.2% warm-up: say 'same loop', never 'same recipe'
Hugging Face reference numbers are the run_glue README results for bert-base-CASED (one seeded run); we use bert-base-uncased
The paper labels test (Table 1) and dev (Tables 5-7) correctly; the weakness is that small tasks (RTE, CoLA, STS-B) are reported on test only, so they cannot be checked on dev
The r-metrics CoLA animation shows 57.3 from re-scoring the saved seed-1 visualisation checkpoint; the main seed-1 log says 56.8; table mean 57.8 over 3 seeds
